name: Cerebral folate deficiency
aliases: neurodegeneration due to cerebral folate transport deficiency

reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Defined biochemically by a low cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) concentration despite normal peripheral folate status
The hereditary form is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FOLR1, encoding folate receptor alpha, which mediates folate transport across the choroid plexus into the central nervous system
Typically presents in late infancy with developmental regression, irritability, movement disorder, acquired microcephaly, ataxia and drug-resistant seizures
Folinic acid (a reduced folate that can bypass the transport defect) is the specific treatment and can improve or stabilise neurological function, especially when started early
Some children have a leukoencephalopathy or hypomyelination on MRI that may partly reverse with treatment
Folate receptor autoantibodies and secondary causes (mitochondrial disease, Kearns-Sayre syndrome) can produce an acquired cerebral folate deficiency phenotype
Standard oral folic acid is not the correct therapy; reduced folate is needed to restore central nervous system folate
Lumbar puncture for CSF 5-MTHF is central to diagnosis and should be considered in unexplained infantile regression with movement disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Cerebral folate deficiency is a state of low central nervous system folate in the presence of normal systemic folate. In the hereditary FOLR1 form, loss of functional folate receptor alpha at the choroid plexus prevents transport of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate from blood into cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting central folate deficit impairs one-carbon metabolism, methylation reactions and neurotransmitter synthesis in the developing brain, leading to hypomyelination, neuronal dysfunction and a progressive encephalopathy. Because folinic acid is a reduced folate that can reach the brain through alternative routes, supplementation can raise CSF folate and mitigate the neurological damage.
additionalDifferentials: Rett syndrome and other regression syndromes
Inborn errors of folate metabolism (e.g. DHFR or MTHFR deficiency)
Autoimmune (folate receptor antibody) cerebral folate deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Serum and red-cell folate to confirm normal peripheral status
Brain MRI for hypomyelination or leukoencephalopathy
reference.prognosis: Early folinic acid treatment can arrest regression and improve development, but delayed diagnosis is associated with irreversible neurological impairment, so outcome is strongly time-dependent.
pitfalls: Measuring only peripheral folate, which is typically normal, and thereby missing the diagnosis
Treating with plain folic acid instead of a reduced folate such as folinic acid
Attributing the picture to non-specific epileptic encephalopathy without CSF studies
Failing to distinguish hereditary FOLR1 disease from autoantibody-mediated or mitochondrial secondary forms
references: GeneReviews: FOLR1 Deficiency (Cerebral Folate Transport Deficiency)
